title: Photosynthesis Impostor: Who's Faking It?
briefing: Everyone gets a fact card, but one card is secretly fake. Read yours aloud, defend it, grill your friends, and vote out the impostor!
intro: Five rounds, from leaf colors to cactus tricks. One card each round is lying. Trust no one (except chlorophyll).
outro_win: Impostors caught! Your photosynthesis brain survived the grilling.
outro_lose: The impostors got away with it. Check each round's fake and why it's wrong, then demand a rematch.

true_facts: Pigments sit in the thylakoid membranes, grouped around each photosystem so they can pass energy inward.
Chlorophyll b and carotenoids pass their absorbed energy to chlorophyll a, so more light gets used.
When a pigment absorbs a photon, one electron jumps to a higher energy level because it gained energy.
Carotenoids protect chlorophyll from too much light, so leaves in bright sun don't get damaged.
In autumn, leaves turn yellow because chlorophyll breaks down first and reveals the carotenoids underneath.
Chlorophyll in a test tube glows red, because its excited electrons fall back with nothing to catch them.
Light energy gets stored because the reaction center hands its excited electron to an acceptor molecule.
A mix of pigments lets a leaf catch more colors of light, since each pigment absorbs different ones.
Photosystem II's center is named P680 because its chlorophyll absorbs best at 680 nanometers.
Brighter light speeds up the light reactions, because it excites more electrons per second, up to a limit.
rounds.corrupted_fact: Leaves look green because chlorophyll absorbs green light best and uses it to power photosynthesis.
rounds.correct_version: Leaves look green because chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects most of the green light.
rounds.explanation: You see the color a pigment does NOT absorb. Chlorophyll soaks up red and blue, so green bounces back to your eyes.

rounds.topic: Electron flow in the light reactions
true_facts: Photosystem II hands its excited electrons to plastoquinone, which carries them across the thylakoid membrane.
The cytochrome complex uses energy from passing electrons to pump H+ into the thylakoid lumen.
Photosystem I re-energizes electrons with a second photon, so they have enough energy to make NADPH.
NADP+ reductase adds two electrons and an H+ to NADP+, so NADPH forms at the end of the chain.
Electrons travel from Photosystem II to Photosystem I, because PSII's electrons are what refill PSI.
Plastocyanin is a small copper protein that ferries electrons from the cytochrome complex to Photosystem I.
In cyclic flow, Photosystem I sends electrons back to the cytochrome complex, so it makes ATP but no NADPH.
The light reactions run in the thylakoid membranes, because that's where the photosystems are built in.
Electrons lose a bit of energy at each step, like a ball bouncing down stairs, which powers the pumps.
The weed-killer DCMU blocks electrons from leaving Photosystem II, so NADPH production in the leaf stops.
rounds.corrupted_fact: The oxygen gas from photosynthesis comes from splitting carbon dioxide, which happens in the Calvin cycle.
rounds.correct_version: The oxygen gas from photosynthesis comes from splitting water molecules at Photosystem II.
rounds.explanation: Tracer experiments show labeled oxygen in water, not CO2, ends up as O2 gas. CO2's oxygen ends up in sugar and water.

true_facts: Bright light drops the lumen to about pH 5 while the stroma stays near 8, because H+ piles up inside.
The H+ gradient stores energy like water behind a dam, so letting H+ flow back out can do work.
ATP synthase spins like a tiny turbine because hydrogen ions rush through it, and the spinning makes ATP.
Chloroplasts make ATP the same way mitochondria do, since both use an H+ gradient across a membrane.
Splitting water inside the lumen releases H+ right there, which adds to the gradient.
If the thylakoid membrane leaks H+, electrons still flow but ATP output drops, since the gradient collapses.
The cytochrome complex pumps H+ into the lumen, so electron flow keeps building the gradient.
ATP synthase releases ATP into the stroma, which is handy because the Calvin cycle runs there.
Linear flow makes slightly too little ATP for the Calvin cycle, so cyclic flow tops it up.
Making NADPH uses up H+ in the stroma, which makes the gradient across the membrane even steeper.
rounds.corrupted_fact: ATP synthase makes ATP as H+ flows from the stroma into the lumen, because that way is downhill.
rounds.correct_version: ATP synthase makes ATP as H+ flows from the lumen out into the stroma, down its gradient.
rounds.explanation: H+ gets pumped INTO the lumen, so the lumen is the crowded side. ATP synthase spins as H+ rushes back OUT to the stroma.

true_facts: In fixation, Rubisco sticks CO2 onto a five-carbon sugar called RuBP, so carbon enters the cycle.
The six-carbon product is unstable, so it instantly splits into two three-carbon 3-PGA molecules.
ATP and NADPH from the light reactions turn 3-PGA into G3P, which is the cycle's sugar.
Three CO2 make six G3P, but only one leaves as sugar because five must rebuild RuBP.
Five of every six G3P get rearranged back into RuBP, which costs the cycle extra ATP.
One net G3P costs 9 ATP and 6 NADPH, since each CO2 costs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH.
Exported G3P can become glucose, starch, or even amino acids, because it's a flexible building block.
The Calvin cycle runs in the stroma, so ATP from ATP synthase lands right where it's needed.
Without new RuBP, fixation stops fast, because Rubisco runs out of things to stick CO2 onto.
Most of a tree's wood came from CO2 in the air, because the Calvin cycle builds sugar from it.
rounds.corrupted_fact: The Calvin cycle runs mostly at night, because it doesn't need light to fix CO2 into sugar.
rounds.correct_version: The Calvin cycle runs mostly during the day, because it needs ATP and NADPH from the light reactions.
rounds.explanation: "Dark reactions" only means they don't use light directly. They need a steady supply of ATP and NADPH, which runs out soon after dark.

true_facts: Rubisco grabs O2 instead of CO2 more often as leaves heat up, which wastes the plant's energy.
Photorespiration burns ATP and releases CO2 without making sugar, so it drags down growth.
When stomata close on a hot day, O2 builds up inside the leaf, since CO2 can't get in.
PEP carboxylase grabs CO2 even when it's scarce, and it never grabs O2, so it's very reliable.
Cacti open their stomata at night so they lose less water, then store CO2 as acids until morning.
CAM plants separate CO2 capture and the Calvin cycle in time, so stomata can stay shut all day.
In dim light, adding extra CO2 barely helps, because light is the limiting factor.
Past its best temperature, photosynthesis slows because enzymes like Rubisco start losing their shape.
C4 plants spend extra ATP to concentrate CO2, which pays off in hot places but not cool ones.
Rubisco is so slow that plants make tons of it, so it's likely Earth's most common protein.
rounds.corrupted_fact: In C4 plants, Rubisco works in the mesophyll cells, because that's where CO2 is first captured.
rounds.correct_version: In C4 plants, Rubisco works in the bundle-sheath cells, where CO2 captured in the mesophyll gets concentrated.
rounds.explanation: C4 plants split the jobs by place. PEP carboxylase grabs CO2 in the mesophyll, then ships it to bundle-sheath cells so Rubisco gets lots of CO2.
